name: Feature Stores
title: Feature Stores
answer: A feature store is a managed set of tables of model input values, computed once and served identically to training and to production, which prevents a model from being trained on one definition of a value and run on another. It sits between the systems that produce raw data, such as event streams and operational databases, and the systems that consume model inputs, such as training pipelines and live scoring services. The core promise is consistency: the same customer tenure, the same rolling seven day spend, the same category embedding, whether the request comes from a notebook yesterday or an API call this second. It is a data engineering concern as much as a machine learning one, because the hard part is the pipeline, not the model.

sections.body: A feature store is a managed set of tables of model input values, computed once and served identically to training and to production, which prevents a model from being trained on one definition of a value and run on another. It sits between the systems that produce raw data, such as event streams and operational databases, and the systems that consume model inputs, such as training pipelines and live scoring services. The core promise is consistency: the same customer tenure, the same rolling seven day spend, the same category embedding, whether the request comes from a notebook yesterday or an API call this second. It is a data engineering concern as much as a machine learning one, because the hard part is the pipeline, not the model.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A feature store runs on the same storage and compute a data team already operates: a warehouse or lakehouse for the offline tables, a low latency key value store or cache for the online tables, and a scheduler or stream processor to keep both fed. Offline storage holds history for training and backfills, typically in columnar files or warehouse tables, while online storage holds only the latest value per entity key and answers lookups in milliseconds. A registry or metadata service records each feature's definition, owner, type and source, and a transformation layer, often SQL or a dataframe API, expresses how raw columns become feature values. Materialization jobs move computed values from the offline side to the online side on a schedule or continuously, and the two sides must agree on the same transformation logic or the store has failed at its one job.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts by defining entities, such as a customer or a device, and the features attached to them, then writing the transformation that produces each value from source data. Teams typically build features in SQL or a dataframe library, register them with a name, type and description, and let the store manage backfills and scheduled refreshes. Point in time correctness is the discipline that matters most: when building a training set, the store must return the feature value as it stood at the moment of each label, not the latest value, or the model learns from the future. Serving then reads the same definitions from the online store at request time, and monitoring compares live distributions against training distributions to catch drift and pipeline breakage. Backfills, freshness targets and entity keys are the everyday vocabulary of the people who run this.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because a feature store concentrates model inputs in one place, it also concentrates questions of ownership, access and provenance. Each feature needs an owner, a documented definition and a lineage trail back to its source tables, so that a value appearing in a model decision can be explained and reproduced. Access controls usually follow the same roles as the underlying warehouse, with sensitive attributes such as health or financial indicators restricted or transformed before they reach the online store, and audit logs recording who read or changed a definition. Training and serving parity is itself a governance property: if the two paths diverge, the model's documented behavior no longer matches its live behavior. Retention rules, deletion requests and consent terms from the source systems have to propagate through materialized copies, which is easy to overlook once values are cached for fast lookup.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward less duplication and more automation: feature definitions expressed once and compiled to both batch and streaming execution, tighter integration with warehouse catalogs and lineage tools, and vector or embedding features treated as first class alongside numeric ones. Streaming stores and online-offline consistency checks are becoming standard rather than specialist add-ons, and the boundary between a feature store and a general data platform keeps blurring as warehouses add low latency serving. The open questions are less about storage and more about semantics: how to version a feature without breaking every model that depends on it, how to retire features safely, and how to keep cost and freshness in balance as the number of consumers grows. Teams that treat the store as a product with owners and contracts tend to get more from it than teams that treat it as a folder of tables.
